title: The tzimtzum and the reshimu: the Essence hidden in the impression, in order to give
overview:
Chapter 12 explains the first *tzimtzum* and the *reshimu* it left, which the preface calls the main thing in the true unity: everything, even the whole chain of the *Kav*, is as nothing before Him, so that a person gives his will to the Essence alone and is not fooled by the *hishtalshelus*.

The analogies all say one thing. A teacher hides his depth and gives a child only a dot, yet the whole *pilpul* is in his mind and in the short law, as the Gemara is in the Mishna. The soul shrinks itself to live in the body, and its *tzelem* stays whole, as the phantom limb shows. The *reshimu* goes further: a blueprint, a sign, a thrown stone, a hint of the hand, a letter thrown across two hundred years, each more removed and each still carrying the self. Rabbi Markel adds an analogy of his own, the impression on a detective's notepad, and the seal in the wax, whose hollow is exact and backwards. And the point he presses most: the *tzimtzum* is not to withhold but *davka* to give, until the student is a Rebbe like his teacher. "A very big promise."

terms.gloss: contraction; here not a real one, since nothing is lost and it is done in order to give
the impression left after the tzimtzum: a withdrawal in which only a trace is left, and yet the whole self is in it
the giver, the teacher, who hides his depth in himself
the receiver, the student, for whose sake the contraction is made
an impression, a mark: the dot left of the teacher's depth, or the craftsman's sketch
Talmudic debate; the whole Gemara included in the short law of the Mishna
shortening; the Mishna, the little that holds the much, which is not yet a real tzimtzum
the form; more than an image: the whole form of the person, present from the first cell
a sign made as a reminder, like an acrostic or initials; unrelated to the thing itself
a hint, like a string around the finger or a movement of the hand, with nothing of the thing in it
a reversing seal: the hollow it leaves in wax has its exact shape, backwards
this opposite that; the reshimu as the inverted image of the original, the yetzer hara

sections.title: Preface: the tzimtzum and the reshimu are the heart of the true unity
sections.summary: The chapter turns to the first *tzimtzum* and the *reshimu* it left. Understanding them in depth is the main thing in the true unity: that everything, the whole chain of the *Kav*, is as nothing before Him, so that a person gives his will to the Essence alone and is not fooled by the *hishtalshelus*.

phrases.he: (יב) ומעתה יש להבין ביאור ענין הצמצום הראשון הנזכר לעיל
ובחינת הרשימו שנשאר כו'
הגם שידוע ליודעים,
phrases.en: even though in general people know about this,

phrases.he: הרי יש בזה פרטים רבים
וצריך להעמיק הדעת בהם ביותר
כי זהו עיקר היחוד האמיתי בעצמות אור אין סוף
phrases.en: the main thing in understanding in terms of the *yichud* is to understand the *inyan* of the *tzimtzum* and *reshimu*.

blocks.text: Now the *inyan* is going to be the *inyan* of the *tzimtzum* and the *reshimu*. Even though it is known to those who know: in general people know about this. But there are many *pratim* (particulars) in it, and one has to go deep into them, because the main thing in understanding the unity is to understand the *tzimtzum* and the *reshimu*.

phrases.he: איך דכולא קמיה כלא כו',
גם בבחינת כללות כל ההשתלשלות דקו וכו'
עד שיוכל אדם לכוון רצונו במסירת נפש לעצמות אור אין סוף לבדו
כמו שכתוב אתה הוא יהו״ה לבדך, אתה כו',

blocks.text: What one has to see is that everything before Him is as nothing, and not only the details: even the whole of the *hishtalshelus* (chain of descent) of the *Kav*. The point of it is that a person should be able to give his will and his *mesirus nefesh* to the Essence of the *Ein Sof* alone, and not get fooled by the whole *hishtalshelus*. "You are He, *Havaya*, alone."

phrases.he: וזהו המלך המרומם לבדו,
בחינת מלכות דאין סוף שלפני הצמצום
שמתנשא גם מימות עולם דאדם קדמון,
שנקרא ימי קדם הנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: "The King who alone is exalted" is the *Malchus* of the *Ein Sof* before the *tzimtzum*, raised even above the days of *Adam Kadmon*, which are called *yemei kedem*. By the way, as he said before, usually *yemos olam* means *Atzilus*, and *yemei kedem* means the *middos* of *Atik* and *Arich*. Here the text is saying a different thing.

phrases.he: וזהו השמים,
בחינת סובב הכללי שאחר הצמצום
ושמי השמים, שלפני הצמצום,
לא יכלכלוך,
גם בבחינת כלי לכלי,
phrases.en: a *kli* to a *kli*.

phrases.he: כמו גליף גליפו בטהירו עילאה כו'
phrases.en: even a *glif glifu* in the *tehiru ila'a* is not even a *kli* for a *kli* for the actual *Aibershter*.

phrases.he: ודי למבין
וכמו שכתוב מי לי בשמים,
שהוא גם בחינת סובב הכללי שלפני הצמצום שנקרא שמי השמים כו'
ועמך לא חפצתי בארץ,
בבחינת קו וחוט בחינת ממלא הכללי כו'

blocks.text: "The heavens" is the general *sovev* after the *tzimtzum*, and "the heavens of the heavens", before the *tzimtzum*, "cannot contain You". *Yechalkelucha* means a *kli* to a *kli*: even the *glif glifu* in the *tehiru ila'a* is not even a vessel for a vessel for the actual *Aibershter* (G-d).

Then "Whom do I have in heaven?" In other words, here "heaven" is what the previous explanation called "the heavens of the heavens", the general *sovev* before the *tzimtzum*; and "on earth" is the *Kav* and thread, the general *memalei*. That is the preface to the chapter, and now he is going to explain the actual *inyan*.

sections.title: One pattern: the Essence hidden, so that the light can come with a leap
sections.summary: There are several analogies for the *tzimtzum*, but they all say one thing: for the light to flow as a *Kav*, the Essence of the light had to be hidden in itself, with only the merest edge left to shine, so that it can be drawn down by a leap across the gap.

phrases.he: והנה יש כמה אופנים במשלים שונים
להשכיל ביאור ענין הצמצום הנקרא מקום פנוי כידוע למעיין
וכללותו עולה בסגנון א',
phrases.en: But in general it's one *inyan*.

phrases.he: והוא כדי שיוכל להיות אור אין סוף בבחינת השפעה בצמצום בבחינת קו,
הוצרך לצמצם עצמות אורו שישאר בהעלם בעצמותו כו'
ולא יאיר כולו, רק אפס קצהו בלבד
כדי שיהיה אחר כך המשכות האור בדילוג הערך

blocks.text: There are several ways, in different *meshalim*, to grasp the *tzimtzum* called the *makom panui*, but in general it all comes to one *inyan*: for there to be a flow in a contracted way, as a *Kav*, He had to contract the Essence of His light so that it stays hidden in His Essence.

Not all of it would shine, only the merest edge of it, so that afterwards the light can be drawn down *b'dilug ha'erech*, by a leap. "That's the *inyan* of the *tzimtzum* and *reshimu*." And now he is going to give *meshalim*.

sections.title: The first analogy: the teacher's Mishna holds the whole Gemara
sections.summary: A teacher hides his depth in himself and gives a small student only a dot. But it is not a real *tzimtzum*: the whole *pilpul* is in his mind and in the short law, as the Gemara is in the Mishna, and the whole point of the contraction is to give, until the student becomes a Rebbe like him.

phrases.he: והרי זה כמשל אור שכל עמוק ורחב שבעצמות המשפיע
שכדי שיומשך ממנו למקבל הבלתי ערך אליו,
הוצרך המשפיע להעלים בעצמו כל עומק השגתו,
ולא ישאר רק בחינת רושם, כנקודה א',
מכל העומק והרוחב

blocks.text: The first *mashal*: the light of a deep and broad intellect in the *mashpia* himself. For it to come to a *mekabel* who is not on his level at all, the giver had to hide in himself the whole depth of his comprehension, so that only a *roshem* is left, like one dot, of all the depth and breadth.

phrases.he: ולא שנסתלק ונתעלם לגמרי
phrases.en: It's not that it actually disappears,

phrases.he: רק כמו השונה בדרך קצרה,
phrases.en: it's like a Mishna in relationship to the Talmud,

phrases.he: שכל העומק ורוחב הפלפול ישנו בשכלו,
phrases.en: that when he says a Mishna, he knows the whole Gemara on it,

phrases.he: רק שהוא נכלל לפי שעה בהעלם עצמותו
בשעה שאומר הדין דרך קיצור
phrases.en: when he's saying the Mishna in a short way.

phrases.he: ומיד שישאלוהו ירחיב הדבר כו'
phrases.en: The minute somebody will ask him, he'll be able to tell you the whole big *pilpul* on it.

phrases.he: רק בשביל שיובן למקבל דרך זה הקצר, מעלים גם בעצמו לפי שעה כו'
phrases.en: Because he is teaching little children *Mishnayos*, so even inside of himself he is hiding it for the time being,

phrases.he: וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות
phrases.en: like it explains in another place at length.

blocks.text: Not that it went away and was hidden altogether: it does not actually disappear, because this whole thing is happening in the *mashpia* himself. It is like a Mishna in relation to the Talmud. When he says a Mishna he knows the whole Gemara on it; it is only included in him, hidden, for the time being, while he says it in a short way. And the minute somebody asks him, he will be able to tell you the whole big *pilpul* on it.

So that the receiver should understand in this short way, he hides it even in himself for the time being: because he is teaching little children Mishnayos, even inside himself he is hiding it for the time being, as it explains at length elsewhere.

phrases.he: 13 ומה שנשאר כמו נקודה, שהוא דרך קצרה,
phrases.en: And what is left like a *nekuda*, which is a short way,

phrases.he: אין זה צמצום גמור ואמיתי
phrases.en: first of all, it's not a total *tzimtzum*, and secondly, it's not even a real *tzimtzum*,

phrases.he: כמו המצמצם ומעלים לגמרי,
phrases.en: like somebody who actually makes a real *tzimtzum* and totally hides it,

phrases.he: שנחסר למקבל לגמרי
phrases.en: that over there it's missing by the *mekabel* totally.

blocks.text: And what is left like a dot, which is the short way, is not a total and real *tzimtzum*. First of all it is not a total *tzimtzum*, and secondly it is not even a real *tzimtzum*: not like one who contracts and hides altogether, who really makes a *tzimtzum* and totally hides it, so that by the *mekabel* it is totally missing.

And here it is not only that it is not that: it is *mamash* the opposite. The whole reason it is done in the first place is *davka* in order to give it over to the *mekabel*. "It's *davka davka* for that." So not only is it not an actual *tzimtzum kipshuto* (literally), it is really the opposite of a total *tzimtzum*. A *tzimtzum* means that something is going away; this *tzimtzum* is *davka* the opposite, in order to give it. It is not in order to stop it.

blocks.title: One fishy plus one fishy
blocks.text: It is like a teacher with little kids. When he teaches them mathematics he has to *metzamtzem* (contract) the whole thing, and not only that, he has to *megashem* it, make it physical: one fishy plus one fishy, or, like they say, if you have an apple and then another apple, and then if you have four apples and you eat an apple... He has to totally make the *inyan* physical so that they will understand it. In the beginning he can only tell them tiny little things. But the reason he tells them tiny little things is not to withhold the information, just the opposite. He really wants to give them the whole information, so that when they finish first grade they get to second grade, all the way up until they do post-graduate work, and finally they become a Rebbe just like him.

And the final *inyan* of the whole thing with a teacher, the goal, is not just that they will know as much as he does. "That's not the goal. The goal is that they'll be a Rebbe just like him." In other words, the actual *Atzmus* (essence) is going to be given over. When they finish, it is not just that there will be a guy who knows a bunch of knowledge: he will *mamash* have the *etzem* of a Rebbe himself.

phrases.he: אלא הענין הוא שכולל בדרך קצר זה כל האריכות,
לא יחסר דבר וחצי דבר

blocks.text: This short way includes all the length; not a thing, not half a thing, is missing. So this is not even like the *mashal* of a *goyishe* (non-Jewish) school. You have to take *davka* the *mashal* in a Jewish school, because the Mishna is not just a *kitzur* (shortening) that leaves some things out. In the Mishna there is nothing missing at all: the whole Talmud is included in it.

sensitivity.reason: Contrasts a "goyishe" school, whose summaries leave things out, with a Jewish one.
sensitivity.publishable: This short way includes all the length; not a thing, not half a thing, is missing. So this is not like an ordinary summary in school. The *mashal* has to be the Mishna, because the Mishna is not just a *kitzur* (shortening) that leaves some things out. In the Mishna there is nothing missing at all: the whole Talmud is included in it.

phrases.he: כמו שכלול בדין הקצר שבמשנה
כל האריכות הפלפול שבגמרא

blocks.title: Rebbi, the Romans, and the Gemara before the Mishna
blocks.text: Not only that he knows the whole *pilpul*: the real thing is just the opposite. The *pilpul* of the Gemara came out of the Mishna. You know the whole story: Rebbi saw that the Romans were making problems and the yeshivos were getting messed up. Most people think it went one way, first the Mishna and then the Gemara; but really there was a Gemara before the Mishna. They had the whole *Torah sheb'al peh* (Oral Torah) before the Mishna, and he took it and put it in a very short way so that it could be *shone*, gone over very fast. And it is said in such a way that later on, when they forgot certain things, they could reconstitute it out of the Mishna. So you see that the whole previous Gemara was really included in the Mishna, and you can bring the whole *pilpul* of the Gemara back out of it, because it is all included in the *kitzur* of the Mishna.

phrases.he: וכמו שלא נעלם ליודע כל הפלפול
גם בשעה ששונה לעצמו דרך קיצור כו'
שנמצא שידיעתו באריכות מקפת בהעלם כל התגלות הקיצור
ולא שנסתלק לגמרי כשכחה
phrases.en: It's not that it really went away, like he forgot it.

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא כו'
וכמו שכתוב ביאור זה באריכות במקום אחר.

blocks.text: When somebody really knows the whole Gemara, a big real *talmid chacham* like they used to have in the olden days, then even when he says a Mishna he knows the whole thing, as if Rashi were saying a Mishna. His knowledge at length encompasses, hidden, everything revealed in the short version.

It did not go away altogether, as in forgetting. If you forget something, it went away, like somebody who has amnesia, *chas v'shalom* (Heaven forbid). But he knows the whole thing right now, even while he is saying it the short way.

sections.title: The second analogy: the soul's life in the body, the phantom limb and the tzelem
sections.summary: The soul has to hide and shrink itself to become the life of the flesh, yet the physical life stays bound to it: joy and pain are felt in the soul, and when the soul leaves there is no life. A lost limb is not lost to the soul, as the phantom limb shows, because the soul's *tzelem*, the whole form, hovers over the body and is there from the first cell.

phrases.he: ואופן משל הב' מחיות הנפש בגוף
גם כן עולה על דרך הנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: It also comes in the same way.

phrases.he: והוא בהיות שכדי שישתנה מחיי רוחניים שבעצם הנפש לחיי בשר,
הוצרך להיות בחינת העלם וכיווץ האור של הנפש בתחלה
לפי שאין ערך ביניהם
phrases.en: it's a totally different *inyan*.

blocks.text: The second kind of analogy, from the life of the soul in the body, comes out the same way. For the spiritual life of the soul to turn into the life of the flesh, there first has to be a hiding and a shrinking of the light of the soul, because there is no comparison between them. The soul just as it is cannot come into the body.

Even a little piece of the soul, one power of the soul, cannot. As they were talking about before, with Abbott and Costello and the Wolf Man: even the *koach hadibur* (power of speech) or the *koach hatnua* (power of motion), if the whole *koach hatnua* tries to come in, it will not be able to, and there will be no motion. So certainly the whole soul cannot go into the body. First of all it is too infinite for it, and secondly, there is no comparison between them: it is a totally different *inyan*, it has nothing to do with the body.

phrases.he: ועם כל זה הרי מתפעלת הנפש ממקרי הגוף
phrases.en: But nonetheless, the soul is *mispa'el*, it gets excited from what happens to the body.

phrases.he: אם כן גם אור הגשמת החיות
phrases.en: the light of the *hagshamas hachayus*, which is the actual physical life,

phrases.he: תתחבר ונקשר אל אור עצמותה הרוחני
phrases.en: So it's connected.

phrases.he: כצמיחה גשמית
שנקשר בכח הצומח הרוחני כו'
phrases.en: that it's connected to the *koach hatzomeach haruchani*.

blocks.text: And nonetheless the soul is moved by what happens to the body: it is *mispa'el*, it gets excited from what happens to the body. Whether something bad happens or something good, the soul feels it. If so, the light of the life made physical, the actual physical life, is joined and bound to the spiritual. So it is connected.

Just as the Mishna is completely connected to the Gemara, the life of the physical is completely connected to the spiritual, and there are two ways you see it. One: the actual happiness and sadness is really in the soul, not in the body. Two: "dead dogs don't bark". If the soul is not there, there is no life of the flesh; the minute the soul leaves, there is no physical life at all. So they are connected, and the spiritual life is *makif* (encompassing) on the physical life.

blocks.title: The plant out of the ground
blocks.text: Like physical growth, which is bound to the spiritual power of growth: you see that if you take the plant out of the ground, it stops growing.

phrases.he: ובהחתך אבר הגוף
phrases.en: And another proof of this is that if somebody accidentally loses a limb, like an arm or a leg or something like that, *chas veshalom*,

phrases.he: לא יחסר באור וחיות רוחניות של אבר זה
phrases.en: the spirituality of it will not be missing anything.

phrases.he: וראיה מסומא שמוליד שלם כו' כידוע
phrases.en: that somebody who, *chas veshalom*, gets blind, it doesn't mean that from now on all his children will be like that, but rather they are born whole.

blocks.text: Another proof: if somebody accidentally loses a limb, an arm or a leg or something like that, *chas v'shalom*, nothing is missing from the spiritual light and life of that limb. Its spirituality is not missing anything.

The proof is from a blind man. Somebody who, *chas v'shalom*, becomes blind does not have blind children from then on; they are born whole. The same with anybody who loses any other limb. If somebody loses a finger, *chas v'shalom*, that does not mean all the rest of his generations will be missing that finger. Just the opposite: they will actually have the finger.

blocks.title: The phantom limb
blocks.text: And another thing: it is a known thing that people who lose a piece of their body still feel it there. There is a ghost, you know: that is called the phantom limb. They still feel it, and as a matter of fact, some of them even have a problem: it itches and you can't scratch it.

phrases.he: אין זה רק שהרוחניות הוא בהעלם,
וישנו במציאותו,
חופף על חיות הגשמי שבגוף
ונקרא צלם איש כו'
phrases.en: And that's called a phantom person. It's not really a phantom person, it's the *tzelem*.

phrases.he: והיינו על דרך הנזכר לעיל בידיעה שבהעלם כו'
(וכל זה מבואר באריכות במקום אחר)

blocks.text: It is only that the spirituality is hidden; it is there, hovering over the physical life of the body, and it is called the *tzelem* of a man. Call it a phantom person; only it is not really a phantom person, it is the *tzelem*. "I don't know how you say *tzelem* in English": a picture, an image. But it is not really an image; it is more than an image. It is the form. *B'tzalmeinu kidmuseinu*, "in our image, after our likeness", yes, but in Hebrew it means a bit more than that. *Tzelem* means that the whole actual form of the person is there.

And this *tzelem* is included, by a tree too and by a person, already in the first cell. The minute a person is conceived, when there are only one or two cells, if you knew how to look at it, you would see exactly how he is going to look when he grows up. The whole codification is there already: you could see if it is a frog or a person, a dog or a horse, and *mamash* what color his eyes are and how smart he is going to be: not according to the education, but the potential. ("Even to the tiniest detail," a student says. "Even to the tiniest detail, right.") If you knew how, you could even get his fingerprints.

blocks.title: The family with the heart attacks
blocks.text: Someone in the class had heard a news report that day: "I was just listening, they had a whole big article on the news today." They made a study of a family of about a hundred people with a very strong propensity for heart attacks: out of about ten siblings nine have heart trouble, and all their offspring too. They studied their genetic codes and found one little tiny protein missing, and that is why. The one brother who does not have the missing protein does not have the heart attacks, and of the offspring, the ones with the protein missing have heart trouble or are going to have it, and the others do not. And you could really see it from when there was one cell: one tiny protein out of the whole genome. "Yeah, but you'd be able to see it with the first cell." Right, exactly: it is encoded; by the first cell it is already there.

In other words, from the minute of conception, when the male and female parts join together; and not only that, it was really there even before that, only in two pieces. And even before those two pieces were there, it was already included in the genetic makeup of his father and his mother, except that you do not know which pieces he will get from each. So the spirituality, the form, the *tzelem*, is already there before that. All this is explained at length elsewhere.

sections.title: More of the same: the power of motion, and being smart
sections.summary: The spiritual power of motion has to contract itself to come into physical motion, or there is no motion at all, as with a man who freezes in fright; and the same holds for many other things, like the smartness of a particular intellect.

phrases.he: וכן כח התנועה הרוחניות כשבאה בתנועת הגשם,
מתצמצמת בעצמותה כו'
ועם כל זה התנועה גשמית מחוברת ומקושרת בתנועה הרוחנית
וכהאי גוונא באופנים אחרים
phrases.en: this is exactly the same *mashal* you can say in many different ways,

phrases.he: כמו ענין התחכמות שכל פרטי מכח המשכיל שלו ששורה עליו בהעלם כו'.

blocks.title: The dinosaur in the street
blocks.text: So too the spiritual power of motion, when it comes into the motion of the physical, is contracted in its essence. As they were talking about before: a guy is walking down the street and all of a sudden a dinosaur comes up. If there is no *tzimtzum* of the spiritual motion when it comes into the physical motion, there will be no physical motion. He'll freeze. He freezes up and cannot make any motion at all.

blocks.title: Calm down and you'll be able to tell me
blocks.text: The same when a guy is very excited: say he just saw the Twin Towers fall, or something like that, and the cop is telling him, "Calm down for a minute, and you'll be able to tell me." What is the cop trying to do? He is trying to make a *tzimtzum*, so that the man will be able to get the speech out of the *koach hadibur*.

And the same in other ways: exactly the same *mashal* can be said in many different ways, like *hischakmus* (being smart) in a particular intellect, from the power of his mind, which was there in him hidden, and all kinds of other things.

sections.title: The reshimu: the blueprint and the sign
sections.summary: The *reshimu* means a withdrawal, with only an impression left. The analogies go down by steps, which a later discourse matches to the four worlds: the Mishna is the same thing as the Gemara; a blueprint is a different thing with the whole shape in it; a sign, like lecture notes or an acrostic, only reminds, and is unrelated to the thing itself.

phrases.he: ואמנם להבין בחינת הרשימו
שענינו מורה בחינת הסתלקות בהעלם
ולא נשאר מהכל רק רושם כו'

blocks.text: But to understand the *reshimu*, whose very meaning shows a withdrawal into hiding, and that nothing at all is left but an impression. The first things were not really that. In the Mishna, even though it is a *kitzur*, it is the same *inyan* as the Gemara. It is what they call *hamu'at hamachzik es hamerubeh*, the little that holds the much; it is not that it is totally gone. That is first of all. Secondly, it is the same *inyan*.

blocks.title: Four analogies in a later discourse
blocks.text: By the way, he was reading in a discourse, of the year 5679 he thinks ("I can't remember... I have to look at the book again"), and it says there are basically four *inyanim* here. One of them is the Mishna and the Gemara; the next is the *reshimas oman*, the craftsman's sketch. There he says there are four *meshalim*, but really you see more than four [here]. The life of the soul and the life of the body, though, is also a small thing that holds a big thing: the motion is a different *inyan*, but it is still the motion included in the original motion. It is not a total removal; something is left over. So: first the Mishna, then the blueprint, then the *os*, like an acrostic, and the last one is a *remez* (a hint). And then he says that the throwing is the actual *inyan* of the *reshimu*: that is a separate thing.

blocks.title: The analogies and the four worlds
blocks.text: And he says that the four are like the four worlds. *Atzilus* is like a *kitzur*: it is still the same *inyan* as the *Atzmus*, even though it is a big *kitzur* of it. And the *remez* is a totally different *inyan*, and that is like *Asiya*. In between he names *Beriya* as the *roshem* and *Yetzira* as "like a map of a big thing", where the *tzura* (form) is still there, and he speaks of the *tziyunim* (markers), like *rashei teivos* (initials), where the thing is already *mamash* gone but the first letter is left over; which analogy goes with *Beriya* and which with *Yetzira* is not clear on the tape.
It is an interesting thing: when you read the Rebbe Rashab, he fills in stuff from here. But you have to know it over here first, before you read it over there.

Not only that: over here we do not necessarily have to know exactly how it applies in the four worlds. What you see over here is that there are different *meshalim*, and one gives you, as in the Mishna and the Gemara, how the whole thing is *mamash* there and nothing at all is missing. "Nothing at all. It's *mamash* the whole Gemara is right there in the Mishna."

phrases.he: הוא מובן יותר מענינים משלים אחרים,
כמו הרושם שעושה האומן
שיוכל לעשות הבנין בקיצור קו זה שברושם,
שכולל כל אריכות המעשה בקיצור רושם זה

blocks.text: It is understood better from other analogies, like the impression (*roshem*) a craftsman makes. He is talking about a blueprint. In this little blueprint is the whole *inyan* of exactly how to build a building: all the length of the work in the brevity of this sketch.

phrases.he: או כמו שעושה לזכרון הנקרא אות
phrases.en: just like an *os*, like a sign.

phrases.he: שאין האות ענין שייך אל עצם הענין,
רק לזכרון בעלמא,
phrases.en: just in order to remember.

phrases.he: כמו עשה לך ציונים כו'

blocks.question: Why is the blueprint not as good a *mashal* as the teacher and the student?
blocks.text: Because it is a different *inyan*. The Mishna is the same *inyan*: there is *chachma* and there is *chachma*. The blueprint is not a building; it is only the shape of a building. With the Mishna, first of all, *mamash* the whole thing is there. That is why it is such a good *mashal*: not even half a thing is missing, and you can reconstitute the whole Gemara out of the Mishna. From the blueprint too you can reconstitute the whole thing, but it is not exactly the same, because it is a different *inyan*. This is a building and this is a drawing.

blocks.question: Is it right to say that the Mishna is the analogy for the *tzimtzum*, showing that the whole thing is included in it, and the blueprint and the others are analogies for the *reshimu*?
blocks.text: No. Later on the text speaks of the *reshimu*: actually the throwing is the analogy for the *reshimu* itself. And the Mishna is also like a *reshimu*. There is a *tzimtzum*, he is *metzamtzem*, and he leaves over a *roshem*. It is a *reshimu*, and it is called a *reshima*.

blocks.title: The notes from the lecture
blocks.text: You know the *Reshimos* of the Rebbe? A *reshima* is when a guy sits in a lecture in school and takes notes. Included in his little notes is the entire lecture, and when he looks at them he will see the whole lecture. Where is the whole lecture? "I don't see the whole lecture." But because he wrote it for himself, in a short way that he understands, when he looks at it he will remember the whole lecture. And that is like the next *inyan* here.
That is like what one makes as a reminder, called an *os*: not just notes, even less than notes, only a sign. The sign has nothing to do with the thing itself.

blocks.title: Every Good Boy Does...
blocks.text: Like when a man ties a string around his finger, though that is really an *inyan* of a *remez*. An *os* is like *tziyunim*, like *rashei teivos*. Or the passage you read on Pesach, where, as it says, what's his name made *tziyunim* in it: *Detzach Adash B'achav*. That is like *rashei teivos*, but not just *rashei teivos*; it is made into a thing. And there is also "Every Good Boy...", what is it? "Is it the colors of the rainbow or something like that?" You make up a little nonsense verse. There are various things to make *tziyunim* to remember something by. "Every Good Boy Does..."

phrases.he: וזהו בחינת העלם יותר מקיצור ההלכה ששונה וכולל בו הכל
שעל כל פנים שייך ענין הקיצור אל האריכות

blocks.text: This is more hidden than the short law, because there at least the short version belongs to the long. If you find money, there is a whole *pilpul* and all this; but nonetheless the *inyan* is finding money, and that is the actual *inyan*. In the Mishna, that is *mamash* the *inyan* you are talking about. In the *os* it is not the *inyan* at all. It is only to remember.

"I don't know what it's an acrostic for. I think it's green something." Whatever it is, that is the *inyan*: if you do not know what it is for, you cannot figure it out. It is not like the Mishna. With a Mishna, even if you cannot figure out the whole *pilpul* of the Gemara, you know they are talking about a guy who hit another guy, or a donkey that stepped on something. You know the exact *inyan*, and even the short version has the *halacha* in it; you just do not know how they derived it. It says it explicitly: what are they talking about? A donkey. Over here you do not know what they are talking about. "Every Good Boy": it is not talking about good boys, really.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 008 opens by finishing class 007's point on lines 50-51 before it reads line 53.

sections.title: Hidden still more: the thrown stone, the hand's hint, the written word
sections.summary: The real analogy of the *reshimu* is the thrown stone: far from the thrower, yet his whole power of motion, and he himself, is in it, so anyone whose window it broke can sue him. Further away still is a hint with the hand, which has nothing to do with the idea, and the writing that carries a teacher's mind across two hundred years.

phrases.he: ויש עוד אופן ברשימו זו
שהוא מורה ענין הצמצום וההעלם הרבה יותר

blocks.text: And there is another kind of this *reshimu*, which shows the *tzimtzum* and the hiding much more, and this already shows the actual *inyan* of the *reshimu*.

phrases.he: והוא כמו הזורק אבן,
שכח המוליך אותו נבדל מן העצם
ועם כל זה
phrases.en: but nonetheless,

phrases.he: כל כח התנועה מלובש בו בהעלם
אך שהוא בריחוק נבדל ביותר מכחו העצמי שבידו
מה שאין כן כח התנועה עצמה שמניעה בעצמו בגשם
שמלובש בגלוי בגשם ביותר כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: One who throws a stone, where the power that carries it is separate from the self. You see a ball rolling down the street and you know somebody kicked it, but you cannot even see the person anymore.

blocks.title: You broke the window
blocks.text: And nonetheless the whole power of motion is dressed in it, hidden. If the stone comes through your window, you can go and sue the person. Why? Because his power of motion is dressed in the stone, and you can blame him for it. It means that not just the power of motion, but the actual intention of the self is dressed in the stone. He says, "What do you want from me? The stone broke your window." "No, you broke the window." "What do you mean I broke the window? I wasn't even there. I was far away from your window. I never went anywhere close to your window." "Doesn't matter. You broke the window." Or, like that song, "I Shot the Sheriff": what do you mean I shot? I didn't shoot the sheriff, the bullet got the sheriff. But you say that you yourself broke the window. So not just the power of motion: the actual *etzem* is dressed in it.

Only it is far away, very separate from his essential power in his hand, unlike when he is actually moving something he is holding in his hand: then it is actually connected to it. In other places in *Chassidus* this *mashal* is given for *Malchus* and *Malchus* of *Malchus*. *Malchus* is when he is actually holding the thing in his hand, and *Malchus* of *Malchus* is when he throws it away.

phrases.he: ויש בחינת העלם יותר גם מזה,
phrases.en: There's an even bigger *helem*,

phrases.he: שדומה לענין הרושם לזכרון לבד
phrases.en: like a *roshem* just for a remembrance.

blocks.text: There is a hiding even greater than this: the impression made only as a reminder. Not like an acrostic. An acrostic, *rashei teivos*, still has something of the thing: those are the letters, and you know it is telling you words that begin with them. This is like a string around your finger, which is only a *remez*. The string does not tell you, "Oh, it must be something to do with strings." It has nothing at all to do with string.

phrases.he: והוא כמו הרומז בידו לאיזה שכל עמוק ביותר
phrases.en: that a very heavy *sechel* can be enclothed.

phrases.he: שנבדל תנועה גשמית מהשכל הרוחני,
ועם כל זה מבין השכל מתוכו כו'

blocks.text: One who hints with his hand at some very deep idea: a very heavy *sechel* can be dressed in it. The physical motion is separate from the spiritual idea, and nonetheless one understands the idea from it.

blocks.title: The Rebbe's hand at the farbrengen
blocks.text: Like when the Rebbe used to make the *chizuk* with his hands during a *farbrengen*: the Rebbe would go like this, and everybody would freak out. "What are you freaking out for?" "Don't you see what the Rebbe is telling us?" "He's not telling you nothing, he's moving his hand." He's saying, "Oh, be strong!" You know what I'm talking about? The thing that the Rebbe used to do.

Or the V-sign; though the V-sign is not really like that, because the V-sign is actually a letter: V for victory. "That's the funny thing": by the hippies it became peace. It doesn't mean peace. It means exactly the opposite of peace, it means winning the war: *netzach*, to win. So it is not a *remez*. It is what was said before, a *tziyun*, *rashei teivos*.

sensitivity.reason: A jab at the hippies for turning the victory sign into a peace sign.
sensitivity.publishable: Or the V-sign; though the V-sign is not really like that, because the V-sign is actually a letter: V for victory. It means winning the war: *netzach*, to win. So it is not a *remez*. It is what was said before, a *tziyun*, *rashei teivos*.

blocks.text: And there are various things like that: you blink your eye to tell a guy something, and all kinds of movements, where the movement has nothing to do with the concept, and yet he understands the concept from it.

phrases.he: ויותר מזה העלם אור השכל בתנועת האצבע בכתיבתו אותו
phrases.en: And even more than that is the light of the *sechel* which is enclothed in the movement of the finger when it writes it,

phrases.he: וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות

blocks.text: And more than this is the hiding of the light of the intellect in the movement of the finger as one writes it: when it writes, it is writing down the *sechel*, and yet it is just a motion.

blocks.title: A stone thrown across two hundred years
blocks.text: And really there is another one even farther away, a combination of the two: when you write a letter. While you are writing, while your hand is actually moving, it is connected: that is *Malchus*. But then you can take it, like a stone, and throw it over two hundred years, which is what we have here in front of us. The Rebbe wrote this down, and then he threw it, not only through space but through time, and it came to us. And in these *reshimos*, the letters themselves have nothing in them. They are pieces of ink on paper, copied from other ink on paper, copied from something a person copied from the manuscript, and then photographed: a *reshimu* of a *reshimu* of a *reshimu*. And yet the whole *sechel* is dressed in it.

sections.title: It all says one thing: a contraction in order to give, and the seal in the wax
sections.summary: Every analogy says that the Essence itself stays, hidden, in the impression, and that the contraction is not one: it is *davka* to give the receiver everything, until the student is a Rebbe like his teacher. Each analogy has what the others lack, and the *reshimu* is like the hollow a seal leaves in wax: exact, and backwards.

phrases.he: והכל עולה לסגנון א' הנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: All of these things is really telling you only one thing:

phrases.he: שבחינת העצמות נשאר בהעלם וכלול ברושם ונקודה זו כו'
ודי למבין:

blocks.text: All of it comes to the one pattern: all these things are really telling you only one thing, that the Essence remains hidden and is included in this impression. Not just the intellect of it, but the *etzem*, the actual selfness. And that is why you say, "You broke the window."

Now back to the teacher. The teacher making the *tzimtzum* is not doing it to give over a little part; first of all certainly not to hide, and not even only to give over the little part that he gives over. Just the opposite: it is not even to give over his intellect. It is really to give over the *etzem*, that the *talmid* (student) should grow up to be a Rebbe too.

So this is the real *inyan*, and the one pattern is: first, the *tzimtzum* is not a *tzimtzum*; and secondly, it is not in order to contract. Just the opposite. As far as the *mashpia* goes, it is certainly not a *tzimtzum*: when the teacher says the Mishna, he knows the whole Talmud. But really even by the *mekabel* it is not a *tzimtzum*. By the *mekabel*, the whole reason for the *tzimtzum* is *davka* to give over the whole *Atzmus* to him.

And the *nimshal* (what the analogy stands for)? Basically, the *Aibershter* is going to give us that the student will be a Rebbe. He is going to give it all over to us, to the Jew. He is going to grow us up to be just like Him. "And that's the promise over here, basically, in the *tzimtzum*, which is a very big promise."

blocks.question: Why does he use all these analogies, each one progressively less than the one before it?
blocks.text: One of the reasons is what he told them: they represent the *tzimtzumim* in the different worlds. But then, why are the worlds contracted that way, each one less than the world before? And why is each *mashal* less than the *mashal* before?

As far as the *meshalim* go: as they were talking about the other day, from what it says in *Pasach Eliyahu*, the *inyan* of the worlds is an *inyan* of *meshalim*, in order to learn about the *Aibershter*. The *hishtalshelus*, which is what we are learning, how the world is constructed, is a *mashal* all the way down to us.

blocks.question: So each analogy gives a different aspect of the *reshimu*, one the others do not, and taken together they give a fuller picture?
blocks.text: Yes. There are various *inyanim* he wants to give over, and as they say, *lo re'i zeh k're'i zeh*: each one has what the other does not. "You shouldn't take any *mashal* by itself." In the *nimshal* it is truly the whole thing. The Mishna and the Gemara, for instance, give you that the whole thing is there: not a thing, not half a thing, is missing. Nothing is missing, and that is very clear in the first *mashal*.

But what is the problem with the first *mashal*? It is not really a total *tzimtzum*. Even though nothing is missing, it is not actually a *tzimtzum*; it is a *kitzur*, a *mu'at hamachzik*, a small thing that holds a big thing. But it is not a nothing. *Tzimtzum* means it was totally gone and only a *reshimu* is left: not a short version, just a *reshimu b'alma*, a mere impression. The original thing is gone.

blocks.title: The impression on the detective's notepad
blocks.text: "Now this is not in the book, I made this one up." In the detective books, they come in and see a notepad. The page the guy wrote the telephone number or the address on is gone, but on the page under it there is an impression of it, and in the impression is the actual telephone number. In the impression you can see the actual thing: the whole thing is there.

blocks.title: The seal in the wax
blocks.text: A *reshimu* also means a *chosam hamis'hapech* (a reversing seal). You stick the seal into the wax and take it out. Now the seal is gone, and what is left is an empty space. But in the empty space itself there is the exact shape of the seal. Except for what? It's backwards. It is inverted: *zeh l'umas zeh* (this opposite that).

So actually the *reshimu* is *mamash* the *yetzer hara* (the evil inclination). The bad is the *reshimu*; the *l'umas zeh* is the *reshimu*. That is what was left in the *chalal* (the space), backwards. What does backwards mean? Where in the original it is in, in the *reshimu* it is out, and where in the original it is out, in the *reshimu* it is in. Everything is backwards, and reversed too.

blocks.title: A mold of a mold
blocks.text: Like how they make a face: they put plaster on the guy's face, or a mold, and take it off. There is a face, but exactly the opposite: where it went out it goes in, and where it goes in it goes out. So what do you do? You put another thing into that, you take a mold of the mold, and it comes out straight.

"So that's how it is. By going away from evil, you're going towards the good." By reversing the *l'umas zeh* you are going towards the *Aibershter*, *mamash* the same, because it is *mamash zeh l'umas zeh*. You make a stamp and take it out, and what is left is the exact opposite: where it is good it is bad, and where it is bad it is good. What in the original says it is good, in the *l'umas zeh* says it is bad. The *l'umas zeh* says, "Oh, I don't want to get married. I want to just hang out." In the original it is the exact opposite, *mamash* opposite.

That is *mamash* the *reshimu*, the *chosam hamis'hapech*: an empty space is left, and in it an exact *reshimu*, backwards from the original. When he leaves the face cast, the empty space is in the exact shape of his face, except backwards. "Except it's not really backwards." The empty space is the exact shape of his face; it is the borders that are backwards. In the seal, too, the space is the same shape. It is the *kli* that is backwards. That too is what a *reshimu* means: an impression, of a seal.

Back to these *meshalim*. The first has it that it is all there. The second gives a better idea: it is not really a house, and yet you can reconstruct the whole house from it. But it is still too much: it is no longer the same *inyan*, but the whole shape is exactly like the original. The third, you *mamash* cannot reconstruct unless you are the original guy and know what it is. And in the fourth it is not even that. So the fourth gives the best idea that it is totally *nivdal* (separate). And really everything is there, because in the final *remez* the whole thing is really there, only it is not so clear as in the Mishna and Gemara. "And that's the reason why."

reviewQuestions.question: Why is the teacher's dot "not a total and real *tzimtzum*", and what is the goal of the contraction?
In what sense was the Gemara before the Mishna, and what does that show about the short way?
What do the phantom limb and the first cell show about the *tzelem*?
Why is an *os* more hidden than the short law of the Mishna?
How does suing the thrower for the stone through the window show that the self is dressed in the thrown stone?
What does the seal in the wax add to the meaning of *reshimu*, and what is backwards in it?

notes.text: Class 007 line 8: he says that usually yemos olam is Atzilus and yemei kedem the middos of Atik and Arich, "like I said before"; kept as he said it.
Line 23 begins with "13" in the chapter text (apparently a page or paragraph mark); rendered "[13]".
Line 42 is not read in class (the alignment marks no reading); its phrase is a plain rendering.

The discourse he was reading: he hesitates between several years ("I think it was" 5679, "I have to look at the book again"); later he speaks of the Rebbe Rashab filling in from here. The block says "of the year 5679 he thinks". Its matching of analogies to worlds is garbled in the transcript after Beriya (he names Beriya as the roshem, then speaks of Yetzira and "a map", then of the tziyunim, then the remez as Asiya); the block gives his clear claims (Atzilus the kitzur, the remez Asiya), reports the Beriya and Yetzira words as he says them, and says the matching is unclear on the tape.

"What's his name made tziyunim": the simanim of the plagues in the Haggada are Rabbi Yehuda's; he does not name him and the block does not either. "Every Good Boy Does Fine" is the lines of the treble staff, not the rainbow; he could not remember and the block leaves it so.
The story of Rebbi and the Romans: he misspeaks ("first was the Gemara and then there was the Talmud"); the block gives what he means, that people think the Mishna came first and the Gemara after.
He says one could read even the fingerprints from the first cell; fingerprints are not fully set by the genes. Left as he said it.
The question "why does he use all these meshalim, each progressively lesser" comes after he asks to turn off the tape; taken as a student's, since he answers "Well, why?".

"The Rebbe took this, he wrote this down... and it came to us": in context the author of the book (the Mitteler Rebbe); the block keeps "the Rebbe". In the farbrengen story "the Rebbe" is the Lubavitcher Rebbe.
The two sensitivity flags (the goyishe school, the hippies and the V-sign) are mild; flagged because they are remarks about groups.

The heart-attack story: the transcript does not show who tells it. It opens with "Right, like I was just listening" and someone answers "Yeah, I heard about that"; the teller is probably a student, and the line tying it back to the first cell ("Yeah, but you'd be able to see it with the first cell") probably Rabbi Markel's. The block frames it neutrally.
Line 40's first clause (והיינו על דרך הנזכר לעיל בידיעה שבהעלם כו') is not read in class; only the parenthetical is (alignment confidence 0.462). Its phrase is a plain rendering.
